claims.statement: Icon carry belongs exclusively to the outer guard process: the guard hides the native icons before spawning the `--panel` child and restores them when that child dies, while the panel process never touches desktop icons, so a killed panel (including a forced kill, since `taskkill /T` only clears the downward subtree) leaves the restore chain intact.

Startup-link maintenance runs inside the panel process's `bootPanel()` during boot rather than in the guard, so the process that raises the panel is also the one that writes or deletes `AGENT DECK.lnk`.

Native desktop icons are hidden by sending `WM_COMMAND` (`0x0111`) with `0x7402` to the `SHELLDLL_DefView` window — the same command explorer's View > Show desktop icons issues — through `SendMessageTimeoutW` with `SMTO_ABORTIFHUNG` and a 3000 ms budget; explorer then writes the resulting state back into the `HideIcons` value under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced`.

`findDefView()` looks for the `SHELLDLL_DefView` child of `Progman` first and otherwise enumerates top-level windows (bounded at 2048 iterations) for a `WorkerW` host, because a dynamic-wallpaper host such as Wallpaper Engine reparents DefView under `WorkerW`; the icon list is the `SysListView32` child of that host.

Two separate observations drive the carry: `iconsVisible()` reads `IsWindowVisible` on the desktop `SysListView32` (the view fact, the sole authority for whether a toggle is needed at restore time), while `prefHidden()` queries the `HideIcons` registry value (the user's persistent preference, which decides whether this run may hide icons at all and is only recorded afterwards).

`IconCarry.begin()` hides icons only when the user does not already prefer them hidden, records one of `icons-hidden` / `icons-already-hidden` / `icons-hide-failed` together with the preference and the post-toggle view state, and a hide failure such as an unreachable `SHELLDLL_DefView` never blocks the panel from being raised — the run degrades to a visible two-desktop state that is recorded in evidence.

`IconCarry.restore(reason)` is idempotent via a `settled` flag and flips the state back only when this run hid the icons and the view is still hidden, so a user who re-shows the native icons while the panel is running is never overridden.

`restoreIfHidden()` deliberately drops the "this run hid them" marker and decides on the view fact alone, because it runs after the guard is dead when that marker is unknowable; a visible list view is never toggled.

The invariant behind every restore path is that the application must never leave an empty desktop: ADR-0004 records restoring the native desktop icons after a crash as a consequence of choosing the Electron panel, and both the ownership-gated and the view-fact-gated restore exist to satisfy it.

The guard restores icons through three in-process paths — `panel-exit` when the panel child exits (called before `app.exit(code)`, which does not run the normal quit sequence), `panel-spawn-failed` when the child cannot be spawned, and `outer-quit` on the guard's `before-quit` event — all routed through the idempotent, ownership-gated `IconCarry.restore`.

When, and only when, this run actually hid the icons (`carry.didHide()`), the guard spawns `icon-restore-watch.cjs` before the panel child with `detached: true`, `stdio: 'ignore'`, `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1` and `unref()`, giving the watcher no console to receive signals from and taking it out of the Chromium kill-on-close job; a spawn failure is logged as `restore-watch-spawn-failed` and the watcher's pid as `restore-watch-spawned`.

The restore watcher opens the guard's process object with `SYNCHRONIZE | PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` and blocks in `WaitForSingleObject(handle, INFINITE)` — waiting on the handle rather than polling the pid makes pid reuse harmless, and an open failure counts as "guard is dead" — then, if the icons are still hidden, calls `restoreIfHidden(null, 'guard-dead')` and always exits 0; the `null` log means the watcher's restore produces no evidence-log event.

`electron . --icon-restore` guarantees the icons are visible in one shot: that mode branch runs before any single-instance logic (so it needs no lock and works while a panel is running), calls `forceShowIcons` and exits 0; `forceShowIcons` toggles only when the `HideIcons` registry preference says hidden — the opposite key from the guard-side restore paths, which use the view fact.

The desired Startup shortcut points at `process.execPath` with the quoted app directory as its only argument and the app directory as working directory, so a Startup boot takes the default entry — the outer guard — rather than `--panel` or `--accept`.

The autostart link lives at `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\AGENT DECK.lnk`; `startupDir()` throws when `APPDATA` is unset instead of guessing a path, and the caller degrades that throw into a warning plus an `autostart-failed` event rather than failing the boot.

The Startup folder is used instead of a `Run` registry key because it is the mechanism the previous stack already used and because the entry stays recognizable both in Task Manager > Startup and in the Startup folder.

Whether an existing link already matches is decided by target and arguments only (working directory is written but never compared), after de-quoting the arguments and lowercasing the target with forward slashes folded to backslashes; production-run path comparison additionally tolerates a trailing separator, so a declared and a running app directory differing by one `\` count as the same place.

`decideAutostart` resolves to `remove` when autostart is disabled and a link exists, `disabled` when disabled with no link, `keep`/`existing-matches` on an exact match, `keep`/`live-other-location` when the existing link differs but its target still exists, `create` with `dead-target` or `missing` when a non-matching or absent link may be claimed, and `skip`/`not-production-run` otherwise.

The right to create or take over the Startup entry (`mayClaim`) is granted only when `config.autostart.appDir` is non-empty and normalizes to the running app directory; the empty default therefore means a run never claims the machine-level entry, which is what stops a development worktree from pointing the machine's boot at a directory that is deleted when the worktree is torn down.

Legacy retirement is unconditional and precedes the main decision: every name in `LEGACY_STARTUP_LINK_NAMES` (currently `qoder-deck-server-watchdog.lnk`) found in the Startup folder is deleted and reported in `autostart-legacy-removed`, matched by name rather than by target path, even when autostart is disabled or the run is not a production run.

`applyAutostart` logs `autostart-read-failed` and proceeds with `existing = null` when reading the link throws, so in a production run an unreadable-but-present link is treated as missing and rewritten; `applied` is true for the no-write actions (`keep`, `disabled`, `skip`) and only after a successful create/remove, a write exception downgrades it to `applied: false` with `autostart-write-failed`, and the caller wraps the whole call so autostart never blocks the boot.

Shortcut read and write go through `src/main/autostart.ps1`, a standalone script invoked with `powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File` and explicit named parameters (avoiding argument re-parsing through `cmd`, because the app directory routinely contains spaces); only read mode reports absence so write mode can create a missing link, output is a single compressed JSON line, and a non-zero exit is surfaced by `readShortcut()` as a thrown error rather than as "the shortcut does not exist".
Shortcut deletion is deliberately implemented in Node (`fs.rmSync` with `force`, best-effort) instead of in the PowerShell helper, and no COM delete branch exists in the script.

`autostart.ps1` must stay pure ASCII (as must the acceptance helpers `capture.ps1` and `uia-focus.ps1`), because Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a BOM-less script using the system ANSI code page and UTF-8 comments become mojibake that breaks parsing outright; the decision rationale is therefore kept in `autostart.ts` rather than in the script.

Both `autostart.ps1` and `icon-restore-watch.cjs` are outside the `tsc` build and are copied into `dist/main` by `scripts/copy-assets.mjs`, landing next to the compiled code that resolves them through `__dirname`.

`bootPanel()` fixes the start-up order as: event log, config load (defaults merged with warnings, and a default config.json written when none exists), `applyAutostart`, legacy usage-log migration, then kernel start and `panelData.whenReady`; migration must precede the collector so a same-day file cannot receive records in the wrong order, and both machine-level duties fail soft.

Autostart is applied once per panel process start from `config.json` — `enabled` defaults to true and `appDir` to the empty string, both trimmed and merged with warnings for illegal values — so changing either value takes effect on the next start and no runtime toggle exists.

Every carry and autostart event is dropped unless `DECK_EVENT_LOG` is set, since `fileEventLog` returns `null` otherwise and the normal dev scripts do not set it, so this machinery is observable only in an acceptance run or an equivalent hand-launched run.

The recorded vocabulary of this area is `carry-boot` (mode `carry` or `restore`), `icons-hidden` / `icons-already-hidden` / `icons-hide-failed`, `icons-restored` / `icons-restore-failed` with a `reason`, `carry-exit`, `restore-watch-spawned` / `restore-watch-spawn-failed`, `autostart-applied` with link, action, reason and applied, `autostart-legacy-removed`, `autostart-read-failed` / `autostart-write-failed`, and `autostart-failed`.

`app/tests/autostart.spec.ts` splits a pure-logic seam (path derivation, argument quoting, `sameShortcut`, the whole decision table, `isProductionRun`) from a `.lnk` adapter seam that is skipped off Windows and uses a temporary Startup directory with the real `WScript.Shell` COM round-trip under a 15 s timeout; the tests pin legacy removal even in a development run, the no-hijack rule for both live and dead links, idempotence on a second run, and the disabled-removes-the-link rule.

Icon carry has no offline unit test because it is Win32-dependent end to end; the acceptance battery instead asserts real state — `SysListView32` invisible while the panel runs, restoration plus guard exit after a `taskkill /F` of the panel with `icons-restored` (reason `panel-exit`) as the recorded proof, and a `--icon-restore` fallback in teardown after the whole process tree is killed — and it re-implements the DefView probe in `accept/lib/win32.js` rather than importing production code.

The acceptance battery contains no autostart assertion, so a genuine reboot check of the Startup entry is a manual verification step; the recorded acceptance run shows the expected non-claiming outcome (`keep`, reason `live-other-location`) because it ran from a working tree that does not match the declared `appDir`.
